title: Continuous Random Variables
summary: A waiting time, a height, a measurement error: these take values in an interval of the real line, not in a countable set. Probability must now be spread over a continuum, so that individual points get mass zero and intervals get positive mass. The tool is…

intro.x: A waiting time, a height, a measurement error: these take values in an interval of the real line, not in a countable set. Probability must now be spread over a continuum, so that individual points get mass zero and intervals get positive mass. The tool is the density, and sums are replaced by integrals. This chapter develops the theory and the standard continuous distributions, with proofs.

blocks.x: A random variable $X$ is continuous (more precisely, absolutely continuous) if there is a function $f=f_X:\R\to[0,\infty)$, called its probability density function (PDF), such that
F_X(x)=\Prob(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for all }x\in\R.
Necessarily $\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)\,dt=1$.
Let $X$ have density $f$. Then
$\Prob(a<X\le b)=\int_a^bf(t)\,dt$, and $\Prob(X\in B)=\int_Bf(t)\,dt$ for every “reasonable” set $B$ (finite unions of intervals, and their limits);
$\Prob(X=x)=0$ for every $x$; hence $\Prob(a\le X\le b)=\Prob(a<X<b)$;
$F$ is continuous, and $F'(x)=f(x)$ at every point $x$ where $f$ is continuous.

(i) $\Prob(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$ by Theorem 4.8(iv). (ii) By Theorem 4.8(v) the mass at $x$ equals the jump of $F$, which is zero since an integral over an interval of shrinking length $\to0$ tends to $0$ (the integrand is integrable). (iii) The fundamental theorem of calculus.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: a density is not a probability

blocks.x: The value $f(x)$ is not $\Prob(X=x)$ (that is $0$), and $f$ can exceed $1$: the uniform density on $[0,\tfrac12]$ equals $2$. The correct interpretation is
\Prob(x<X\le x+h)=\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt\approx f(x)\,h\quad(h\to0),
so $f(x)$ is “probability per unit length” near $x$. Changing $f$ at a single point (or on a set of length zero) does not change any probability, so a density is determined only up to such changes.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: not every distribution without atoms has a density

blocks.x: “Continuous CDF” and “has a density” are different. The Cantor distribution (the law of $\sum_{k\ge1}2\epsilon_k3^{-k}$ with $\epsilon_k$ fair Bernoulli) has a continuous CDF, no atoms, but is concentrated on the Cantor set (length zero), so no density exists. Moreover, a distribution can be mixed, having both atoms and a density part: for example $\Prob(X=0)=\tfrac12$ and otherwise exponential. The CDF handles all cases uniformly, and Chapter 15 gives the complete classification (Lebesgue decomposition). In this chapter “continuous” always means “has a density”.
If $X$ has density $f$ and $\int\abs xf(x)\,dx<\infty$, then $\Exp[X]=\int_{-\infty}^\infty xf(x)\,dx$. Variance, covariance and moments are defined exactly as before: $\Var(X)=\Exp[(X-\mu)^2]$.
If $X\ge0$ has a density, then $\Exp[X]=\int_0^\infty\Prob(X>t)\,dt$.
Write $x=\int_0^x1\,dt=\int_0^\infty\indic_{\{t<x\}}\,dt$. Then

\Exp[X]=\int_0^\infty x f(x)\,dx=\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_0^\infty\indic_{\{t<x\}}f(x)\,dt\,dx
=\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_t^\infty f(x)\,dx\,dt=\int_0^\infty\Prob(X>t)\,dt.
The interchange of the order of integration is legitimate because the integrand is non-negative (Tonelli’s theorem, Chapter 15).
If $X$ has density $f$ and $g\ge0$ (or $\int\abs{g}f<\infty$), then $\Exp[g(X)]=\int g(x)f(x)\,dx$.
For $g\ge0$, apply Theorem 7.4 to the non-negative variable $g(X)$ and interchange integrals again:

\Exp[g(X)]=\int_0^\infty\Prob(g(X)>t)\,dt=\int_0^\infty\!\!\int\indic_{\{g(x)>t\}}f(x)\,dx\,dt
=\int f(x)\int_0^{g(x)}dt\,dx=\int g(x)f(x)\,dx.
(The tail formula for $g(X)$ holds for any non-negative random variable, by the same computation applied to its distribution.) For general $g$ split $g=g^+-g^-$ and use linearity.

Linearity of expectation, monotonicity and the variance identities $\Var(X)=\Exp[X^2]-\mu^2$, $\Var(aX+b)=a^2\Var(X)$ all hold as in the discrete case (proved in Chapter 15 for all random variables simultaneously).

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: A distribution with no mean: the Cauchy

blocks.x: The standard Cauchy density is $f(x)=\dfrac1{\pi(1+x^2)}$. It integrates to $1$ (since $\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\arctan x\big|_{-\infty}^\infty=\pi$), but

\int_{-\infty}^\infty\abs x\,f(x)\,dx=\frac2\pi\int_0^\infty\frac x{1+x^2}\,dx
=\frac1\pi\ln(1+x^2)\Big|_0^\infty=\infty .

So $\Exp[X]$ does not exist. The principal-value limit $\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^{R}xf(x)\,dx=0$ exists by symmetry, but this is not an expectation (it depends on how the two infinite tails are balanced). The Cauchy law is the standard example of a heavy-tailed distribution; the law of large numbers fails for it (Chapter 9).
Uniform
$X\sim U(a,b)$ has density $\frac1{b-a}$ on $(a,b)$ and $0$ elsewhere. Then

\Exp[X]=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^bx\,dx=\frac{a+b}2,\qquad
\Exp[X^2]=\frac{b^3-a^3}{3(b-a)}=\frac{a^2+ab+b^2}3,
Probabilities are proportional to length: $\Prob(X\in(c,d))=(d-c)/(b-a)$.
Exponential
$X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, $\lambda>0$, has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$. Then $\Prob(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ and $F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$. By the tail integral,
\Exp[X]=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\,dt=\frac1\lambda,
and integrating by parts, $\Exp[X^2]=\int_0^\infty x^2\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx =\frac2\lambda\Exp[X]=\frac2{\lambda^2}$, so $\Var(X)=1/\lambda^2$.

If $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ then $\Prob(X>s+t\given X>s)=\Prob(X>t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$. Conversely, a positive random variable with a right-continuous survival function $G(t)=\Prob(X>t)$ that is not identically $0$ or $1$ on $(0,\infty)$ and satisfies this identity is exponential.

Forward direction: $e^{-\lambda(s+t)}/e^{-\lambda s}=e^{-\lambda t}$. Conversely, the identity gives $G(s+t)=G(s)G(t)$. Put $c=G(1)$. By induction $G(n)=c^n$ and $G(1/m)^m=G(1)$, so $G(n/m)=c^{n/m}$ for all positive rationals. We have $0<c<1$ (if $c=0$ then $G(1/m)^m=0$ forces $G\equiv0$ on the positive rationals and, by monotonicity, on $(0,\infty)$; if $c=1$ then $G\equiv1$). Writing $c=e^{-\lambda}$, $G(r)=e^{-\lambda r}$ for rational $r>0$. Since $G$ is non-increasing and right-continuous, approximating any real $t$ from the right by rationals gives $G(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$.
If $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ then $\lceil X\rceil\sim\mathrm{Geom}(1-e^{-\lambda})$.
$\Prob(\lceil X\rceil=k)=\Prob(k-1<X\le k)=e^{-\lambda(k-1)}-e^{-\lambda k}= (e^{-\lambda})^{k-1}(1-e^{-\lambda})$.
So the exponential is the continuous-time analogue of the geometric distribution: waiting for a “memoryless” event.

The hazard rate $h(t)=f(t)/\Prob(X>t)$ is the instantaneous failure rate given survival to $t$. For the exponential, $h(t)=\lambda$ is constant. A constant hazard is equivalent to memorylessness; increasing hazard models wear-out, and decreasing hazard models early failures.
Gamma
The gamma function is $\Gamma(\alpha)=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x}\,dx$ for $\alpha>0$. Integration by parts gives

\Gamma(\alpha+1)=\int_0^\infty x^\alpha e^{-x}\,dx=\bigl[-x^\alpha e^{-x}\bigr]_0^\infty
+\alpha\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x}\,dx=\alpha\,\Gamma(\alpha),
and $\Gamma(1)=1$, so $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$ for positive integers $n$. Also $\Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi$ (shown in Section 7.3.5).
$X\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$ has density
f(x)=\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x>0 .
It integrates to $1$ by the substitution $u=\lambda x$ in the definition of $\Gamma(\alpha)$. The same substitution gives the moments:

\Exp[X^k]=\frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha+k-1}e^{-\lambda x}\,dx
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+k)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\lambda^k}.

Thus $\Exp[X]=\alpha/\lambda$, $\Exp[X^2]=\alpha(\alpha+1)/\lambda^2$ and $\Var(X)=\alpha/\lambda^2$. For $\alpha=1$ we recover the exponential. For integer $\alpha=n$ the gamma distribution (the Erlang distribution) is the sum of $n$ independent exponentials, as we prove in Chapter 8.
Beta
$X\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$, $a,b>0$, has density

where $B(a,b)=\int_0^1x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}dx$. In Chapter 8 we show $B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$, and then $\Exp[X]=B(a+1,b)/B(a,b)=a/(a+b)$ and $\Var(X)=\dfrac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}$. The beta family models unknown probabilities, and $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)=U(0,1)$.
The normal distribution
$\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi}$.
Let $I$ be the integral. Since the integrand is non-negative, Tonelli’s theorem lets us write

I^2=\int\!\!\int e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}\,dx\,dy=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta
=2\pi\bigl[-e^{-r^2/2}\bigr]_0^\infty=2\pi,
using polar coordinates $(x,y)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ with area element $r\,dr\,d\theta$. Since $I>0$, $I=\sqrt{2\pi}$.
Hence $\varphi(x)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$ is a density, the standard normal density. We write $Z\sim N(0,1)$, $\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x\varphi$ for its CDF (which has no closed form).
If $Z\sim N(0,1)$ then $\Exp[Z]=0$ and $\Var(Z)=1$.

$x\varphi(x)$ is an odd integrable function, so $\Exp[Z]=0$. By parts, using $\varphi'(x)=-x\varphi(x)$: $\Exp[Z^2]=\int x\cdot x\varphi(x)\,dx=\bigl[-x\varphi(x)\bigr]_{-\infty}^\infty +\int\varphi(x)\,dx=0+1=1$.
For $\mu\in\R$, $\sigma>0$, the random variable $X=\mu+\sigma Z$ is said to be $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. Its density follows from the change of variables rule below:
f_X(x)=\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr),
with $\Exp[X]=\mu$ and $\Var(X)=\sigma^2$. Two facts: the family is closed under affine maps, and standardising $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma$ reduces every normal probability to $\Phi$.
For $x>0$,
\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \Prob(Z>x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}x.

Upper bound: for $t\ge x$, $1\le t/x$, so $\Prob(Z>x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(t)\,dt\le\int_x^\infty\frac tx\varphi(t)\,dt =\frac{\varphi(x)}x$, since $\frac d{dt}(-\varphi(t))=t\varphi(t)$. Lower bound: a direct differentiation gives $\frac d{dt}\bigl[(\tfrac1t-\tfrac1{t^3})\varphi(t)\bigr]=-(1-3t^{-4})\varphi(t)$, hence $\int_x^\infty(1-3t^{-4})\varphi(t)\,dt=(\tfrac1x-\tfrac1{x^3})\varphi(x)$. As $(1-3t^{-4})\varphi(t)\le\varphi(t)$, the lower bound follows.
The bounds show that the normal tail decays like $e^{-x^2/2}$, much faster than any exponential; this “thin tail” is why the normal is so well-behaved and so dangerous when real data have fat tails.

sections.title: Functions of a continuous random variable

blocks.x: Let $X$ have density $f_X$, and let $g$ be strictly monotone and differentiable on an open interval $I$ containing the support of $X$, with inverse $h=g^{-1}$. Then $Y=g(X)$ has density
f_Y(y)=f_X\bigl(h(y)\bigr)\,\abs{h'(y)}.

If $g$ is increasing, $F_Y(y)=\Prob(g(X)\le y)=\Prob(X\le h(y))=F_X(h(y))$. Differentiate by the chain rule: $f_Y(y)=f_X(h(y))h'(y)$ with $h'>0$. If $g$ is decreasing, $F_Y(y)=\Prob(X\ge h(y))=1-F_X(h(y))$, so $f_Y(y)=-f_X(h(y))h'(y)=f_X(h(y))\abs{h'(y)}$ as $h'<0$.
When $g$ is not monotone, use the CDF method directly: express $\{g(X)\le y\}$ as an event about $X$.
Let $Y=Z^2$. For $y>0$, $F_Y(y)=\Prob(-\sqrt y\le Z\le\sqrt y)=2\Phi(\sqrt y)-1$. Differentiating,
f_Y(y)=2\varphi(\sqrt y)\cdot\frac1{2\sqrt y}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,y^{-1/2}e^{-y/2},
which is the Gamma$(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ density (the chi-squared law with one degree of freedom). Comparing normalising constants, $\Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi$.
Let $X$ have a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ on its support. Then
if $U\sim U(0,1)$ then $F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$.
(i) For $u\in(0,1)$, $\Prob(F(X)\le u)=\Prob(X\le F^{-1}(u))=F(F^{-1}(u))=u$, which is the $U(0,1)$ CDF. (ii) $\Prob(F^{-1}(U)\le x)=\Prob(U\le F(x))=F(x)$.

Part (ii) is the inverse transform method for simulation (Chapter 17): any distribution can be generated from uniform random numbers. For example if $U\sim U(0,1)$ then $-\frac1\lambda\ln U\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, because $F^{-1}(u)=-\frac1\lambda\ln(1-u)$ and $1-U\overset d=U$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: quantiles when the CDF is not strictly increasing

blocks.x: For general $F$ define the quantile function $F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$. Then $F^{-1}(U)$ still has CDF $F$ (because $F^{-1}(u)\le x\iff u\le F(x)$), but $F(X)$ is uniform only if $F$ is continuous. For discrete $X$, $F(X)$ takes only finitely or countably many values.
Find $c$ so that $f(x)=cx^2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ is a density; compute the mean and variance.
Let $X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. Find the density of $Y=X^2$ and of $Y=e^{-X}$ (the latter is uniform).
A bus arrives with $\mathrm{Exp}(1/10)$ waiting time (mean 10 minutes). You have already waited $10$ minutes. What is the expected additional wait?
Show that for any random variable with $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$, $\Exp[X]=\int_0^\infty\Prob(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty\Prob(X<-t)\,dt$.
Prove $\Exp[X^n]=\int_0^\infty nt^{n-1}\Prob(X>t)\,dt$ for $X\ge0$.
Compute $\Prob(\abs Z>3)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and compare with the bounds of Theorem 7.11. Compute $\Prob(\abs Z>x)$ for the Cauchy.
Let $U\sim U(0,1)$. Show that $\min(U,1-U)\sim U(0,\tfrac12)$.
Prove that the Cauchy distribution is closed under reciprocals: if $X$ is standard Cauchy then so is $1/X$.

(Challenge) Show that if $X$ has density and $\Exp[X]$ exists then $\Exp\abs{X-c}$ is minimised at the median, $c=\mathrm{med}(X)$ with $F(c)=\tfrac12$. (Differentiate $\int\abs{x-c}f(x)\,dx$ in $c$.)
